claim: Colony rugosity is regulated by temperature in V. cholerae strains that naturally lack the master biofilm transcriptional regulator HapR.
source: Here, we show that colony rugosity, a biofilm-associated phenotype, is regulated by temperature in V. cholerae strains that naturally lack the master biofilm transcriptional regulator HapR.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations showing temperature-dependent colony morphology changes in HapR-deficient strains (Figure 1).

claim: The V. cholerae ortholog of BipA is critical for temperature-dependent colony rugosity.
source: Using transposon-insertion mutagenesis, we found the V. cholerae ortholog of BipA, a conserved ribosome-associated GTPase, is critical for this temperature-dependent phenomenon.
evidence: Identified through transposon mutagenesis screen and validated by deletion and complementation experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Loss of BipA alters the synthesis of >300 proteins in V. cholerae at 22°C.
source: Proteomic analyses revealed that loss of BipA alters the synthesis of >300 proteins in V. cholerae at 22°C, increasing the production of biofilm-related proteins including the key transcriptional activators VpsR and VpsT, as well as proteins important for diverse cellular processes.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative label-free proteomics comparing WT and ΔbipA strains (Figure 6).

claim: At low temperatures, BipA protein levels increase.
source: At low temperatures, BipA protein levels increase and are required for optimal ribosome assembly in V. cholerae, suggesting that control of BipA abundance is a mechanism by which bacteria can remodel their proteomes.
evidence: Shown by Western blot analysis comparing BipA-flag protein levels at 37°C and 22°C (Figure 4B).

claim: BipA is required for optimal ribosome assembly in V. cholerae at low temperatures.
source: At low temperatures, BipA protein levels increase and are required for optimal ribosome assembly in V. cholerae, suggesting that control of BipA abundance is a mechanism by which bacteria can remodel their proteomes.
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis showing 50S assembly defects in ΔbipA at 22°C (Figure 5).

claim: V. cholerae forms biofilms both in biotic and abiotic surfaces in the aquatic environment.
source: Vibrio cholerae, the causative agent of the severe human diarrhoeal disease cholera, forms biofilms both in biotic and abiotic surfaces in the aquatic environment that it inhabits (Alam et al., 2007; Islam et al., 2007; Lutz et al., 2013) and also in the intestine of the human host (Faruque et al., 2006; Silva and Benitez, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: V. cholerae forms biofilms in the intestine of the human host.
source: Vibrio cholerae, the causative agent of the severe human diarrhoeal disease cholera, forms biofilms both in biotic and abiotic surfaces in the aquatic environment that it inhabits (Alam et al., 2007; Islam et al., 2007; Lutz et al., 2013) and also in the intestine of the human host (Faruque et al., 2006; Silva and Benitez, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Biofilm formation by V. cholerae provides protection against environmental insults, predators, and stress conditions.
source: Biofilm formation by V. cholerae provides protection against environmental insults, predators, and stress conditions and may also promote nutrient access (Lutz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Biofilm formation may promote nutrient access in V. cholerae.
source: Biofilm formation by V. cholerae provides protection against environmental insults, predators, and stress conditions and may also promote nutrient access (Lutz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study, with speculative language ('may').

claim: Biofilm formation is critical for intestinal colonization by V. cholerae.
source: There is some evidence indicating that biofilm formation is critical for intestinal colonization (Silva and Benitez, 2016), and it has been proposed that biofilm formation can enhance the infectivity of V. cholerae (Tamayo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study, with cautious language ('some evidence indicating').

claim: Biofilm formation can enhance the infectivity of V. cholerae.
source: There is some evidence indicating that biofilm formation is critical for intestinal colonization (Silva and Benitez, 2016), and it has been proposed that biofilm formation can enhance the infectivity of V. cholerae (Tamayo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study, with speculative language ('it has been proposed').

claim: V. cholerae's biofilm is primarily composed of Vibrio polysaccharide (VPS), matrix proteins (RbmA, RbmC, and Bap1), and extracellular DNA.
source: V. cholerae's biofilm is primarily composed of Vibrio polysaccharide (VPS), matrix proteins (RbmA, RbmC, and Bap1), and extracellular DNA (Berk et al., 2012; Fong et al., 2006; Fong and Yildiz, 2007; Fong et al., 2010; Reichhardt et al., 2015; Seper et al., 2011; Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The genes encoding VPS production activities are grouped in the vpsI and vpsII clusters.
source: The genes encoding the activities for the production of VPS, grouped in the vpsI and vpsII clusters, and the genes encoding the RbmA and RbmC matrix proteins, located in the rbm cluster between vpsI and vpsII clusters, form the so-called V. cholerae biofilm-matrix cluster (Fong et al., 2006; Fong and Yildiz, 2007; Fong et al., 2010; Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rbm cluster is located between vpsI and vpsII clusters.
source: The genes encoding the activities for the production of VPS, grouped in the vpsI and vpsII clusters, and the genes encoding the RbmA and RbmC matrix proteins, located in the rbm cluster between vpsI and vpsII clusters, form the so-called V. cholerae biofilm-matrix cluster (Fong et al., 2006; Fong and Yildiz, 2007; Fong et al., 2010; Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VpsR and VpsT are the main transcriptional activators of the vpsI and vpsII clusters.
source: Within this complex regulatory network, VpsR and VpsT, whose regulons extensively overlap (Beyhan et al., 2007), are the main transcriptional activators of the vpsI and vpsII clusters and the rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes encoding the matrix proteins (Zamorano-Sánchez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VpsR and VpsT are the main transcriptional activators of rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes.
source: Within this complex regulatory network, VpsR and VpsT, whose regulons extensively overlap (Beyhan et al., 2007), are the main transcriptional activators of the vpsI and vpsII clusters and the rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes encoding the matrix proteins (Zamorano-Sánchez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The regulons of VpsR and VpsT extensively overlap.
source: Within this complex regulatory network, VpsR and VpsT, whose regulons extensively overlap (Beyhan et al., 2007), are the main transcriptional activators of the vpsI and vpsII clusters and the rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes encoding the matrix proteins (Zamorano-Sánchez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: HapR is the main repressor of biofilm formation in V. cholerae.
source: HapR is the main repressor of biofilm formation and inhibits transcription of both the activators and the genes encoding the VPS and the matrix proteins (Waters et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: HapR inhibits transcription of biofilm activators and genes encoding VPS and matrix proteins.
source: HapR is the main repressor of biofilm formation and inhibits transcription of both the activators and the genes encoding the VPS and the matrix proteins (Waters et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: HapR regulates virulence factor production in V. cholerae.
source: HapR also regulates other processes, such as virulence factor production, type VI secretion (Kovacikova and Skorupski, 2002; Zheng et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2002), and intracellular c-di-GMP levels (Hammer and Bassler, 2009; Waters et al., 2008), which in turn indirectly affect biofilm formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HapR regulates type VI secretion in V. cholerae.
source: HapR also regulates other processes, such as virulence factor production, type VI secretion (Kovacikova and Skorupski, 2002; Zheng et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2002), and intracellular c-di-GMP levels (Hammer and Bassler, 2009; Waters et al., 2008), which in turn indirectly affect biofilm formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HapR regulates intracellular c-di-GMP levels in V. cholerae.
source: HapR also regulates other processes, such as virulence factor production, type VI secretion (Kovacikova and Skorupski, 2002; Zheng et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2002), and intracellular c-di-GMP levels (Hammer and Bassler, 2009; Waters et al., 2008), which in turn indirectly affect biofilm formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HapR expression is controlled by the quorum sensing cascade that responds to cell density.
source: HapR expression is controlled by the quorum sensing (QS) cascade that responds to cell density (Hammer and Bassler, 2009; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003), as well as by additional QS-dependent (Lenz and Bassler, 2007; Liang et al., 2007; Shikuma et al., 2009; Tsou et al., 2011) or QS-independent (Liu et al., 2006; Yildiz et al., 2004) regulators.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: V. cholerae experiences a wide range of temperatures in the aquatic environment, ranging between 12 and 30°C.
source: Specifically, V. cholerae experiences a wide range of temperatures, including seasonal and inter-annual temperature changes in the aquatic environment (ranging between 12 and 30°C; Townsley et al., 2016), and also upon infection of the human host (37°C).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: V. cholerae experiences 37°C upon infection of the human host.
source: Specifically, V. cholerae experiences a wide range of temperatures, including seasonal and inter-annual temperature changes in the aquatic environment (ranging between 12 and 30°C; Townsley et al., 2016), and also upon infection of the human host (37°C).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of human body temperature.

claim: Temperature up-shift controls the expression of virulence factors in V. cholerae upon entering the human host.
source: Once V. cholerae enters the human host, the temperature up-shift controls the expression of virulence factors (Parsot and Mekalanos, 1990; Weber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rugose colony-forming V. cholerae El Tor clinical isolate co969 formed smooth colonies when cultured below 22°C.
source: We noticed that the rugose colony-forming V. cholerae El Tor clinical isolate co969 (Figure 1A) formed smooth colonies when cultured below 22°C (Figure 1B), suggesting a role for temperature in the regulation of this phenotype.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations at different temperatures (Figure 1B).

claim: Temperature-dependent rugosity in co969 was not dependent on culture time or culture density.
source: Temperature-dependent rugosity was not dependent on culture time or culture density, as even at extended culture periods (up to 4 days) and comparable culture densities as 37°C cultures, c0969 V. cholerae did not form rugose colonies at 22°C (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU measurements and extended culture experiments (Figure 1D).

claim: V. cholerae co969 naturally lacks wild-type HapR due to a frameshift mutation that results in a truncated version of the protein.
source: V. cholerae co969 naturally lacks wild-type (WT) HapR due to a frameshift mutation that results in a truncated version of the protein (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence analysis (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 1C).

claim: Other V. cholerae WT strains with inactive HapR variants exhibited temperature-dependent rugosity in both solid–air and air–liquid interfaces.
source: We observed that, similarly to co969, other V. cholerae WT strains with inactive HapR variants also exhibited temperature-dependent rugosity in both solid–air (i.e. colony morphology) and air–liquid interfaces (i.e. wrinkled pellicles; Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology and pellicle biofilm assays (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 1).

claim: HapR-sufficient V. cholerae strains C6706 and A1552 were smooth at all temperatures.
source: However, we did not observe this phenotype in HapR-sufficient V. cholerae strains, such as C6706 and A1552 (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 1), which were smooth at all temperatures.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 1).

claim: Deletion of hapR in C6706 and A1552 led to temperature-dependent rugosity development comparable to naturally hapR-deficient strains.
source: Remarkably, deletion of hapR in these strains led to temperature-dependent rugosity development comparable to the naturally hapR-deficient strains, and complementation of co969 with the WT hapR copy from C6706 (hapRc) negated its development of rugosity at high temperatures (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology of deletion mutants (Figure 1E).

claim: Complementation of co969 with the WT hapR copy from C6706 negated its development of rugosity at high temperatures.
source: Remarkably, deletion of hapR in these strains led to temperature-dependent rugosity development comparable to the naturally hapR-deficient strains, and complementation of co969 with the WT hapR copy from C6706 (hapRc) negated its development of rugosity at high temperatures (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology of complemented strain (Figure 1E).

claim: vpsL was upregulated at 37°C vs. 22°C in co969 colonies.
source: Both vpsL, one of the genes encoding the VPS, and bap1, encoding a biofilm matrix protein, were upregulated at 37°C vs. 22°C (correlating with the phenotypes in Figure 1B), suggesting that colony rugosity can be used as a readout in co969 to study temperature-dependent biofilm development regulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR measurements (Figure 2A).

claim: bap1 was upregulated at 37°C vs. 22°C in co969 colonies.
source: Both vpsL, one of the genes encoding the VPS, and bap1, encoding a biofilm matrix protein, were upregulated at 37°C vs. 22°C (correlating with the phenotypes in Figure 1B), suggesting that colony rugosity can be used as a readout in co969 to study temperature-dependent biofilm development regulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR measurements (Figure 2A).

claim: vpsL and bap1 expression did not differ between 37°C and 22°C in the co969:hapRc background.
source: vpsL and bap1 expression did not differ between these two temperatures in the co969:hapRc background, consistent with the idea that the temperature-dependent program governing biofilm development in V. cholerae is enabled in the absence of HapR (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR measurements (Figure 2A).

claim: Expression of the vpsI and vpsII gene clusters was upregulated (~10–20 fold) in 37R compared with 22Sb colonies.
source: Consistent with our phenotypic observations, expression of the vpsI and vpsII gene clusters (e.g. vpsL), encoding the activities responsible for the production of the VPS, and the rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes, encoding the biofilm matrix proteins, were upregulated (~10–20 fold) in 37R compared with 22Sb colonies (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).

claim: Expression of rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes was upregulated (~10–20 fold) in 37R compared with 22Sb colonies.
source: Consistent with our phenotypic observations, expression of the vpsI and vpsII gene clusters (e.g. vpsL), encoding the activities responsible for the production of the VPS, and the rbmA, rbmC, and bap1 genes, encoding the biofilm matrix proteins, were upregulated (~10–20 fold) in 37R compared with 22Sb colonies (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).

claim: Most known biofilm transcriptional regulators were not differentially expressed between 37R and 22Sb colonies.
source: Interestingly, most known biofilm transcriptional regulators (e.g. vpsT, vpsR, and hapR), as well as other genes involved in QS, type II secretion, and c-di-GMP signaling were not differentially expressed (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).

claim: Out of 11,000 mutants screened, 459 colonies had a rugose phenotype at 22°C.
source: Out of 11,000 mutants screened, 459 colonies had a rugose phenotype at 22°C.
evidence: Result from transposon mutagenesis screen.

claim: Pooled sequencing of the 459 rugose colonies identified transposon insertions in 99 genes.
source: Pooled sequencing of the 459 rugose colonies identified transposon insertions in 99 genes, corresponding to diverse cell functions such as flagellar motility, chemotaxis, c-di-GMP signaling, lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, cell wall maintenance, phosphotransferase systems, regulatory functions, transport, and translation (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Result from Tn-seq analysis (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 5).

claim: VC2744 was the most highly represented gene after filtering out potential temperature-independent repressors in co969 rugose colonies at 22°C.
source: The most highly represented gene (frequently inserted gene [i.e. with the largest number of insertion reads]) after filtering out potential temperature-independent repressors in co969 rugose colonies at 22°C was VC2744 (see Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Result from Tn-seq analysis (Supplementary file 5).

claim: VC2744 encodes a protein with 74% identity to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium BipA.
source: VC2744 encodes a protein with 74% identity to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium BipA, also referred to as TypA in other organisms (Leipe et al., 2002; Margus et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in BipA have been associated with a cold-sensitive phenotype in Escherichia coli.
source: Mutations in BipA have been associated with a cold-sensitive phenotype in Escherichia coli (Pfennig and Flower, 2001), but a clean deletion of VC2744 in V. cholerae co969 did not influence growth or cell morphology at low or high temperatures (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A clean deletion of VC2744 in V. cholerae co969 did not influence growth or cell morphology at low or high temperatures.
source: Mutations in BipA have been associated with a cold-sensitive phenotype in Escherichia coli (Pfennig and Flower, 2001), but a clean deletion of VC2744 in V. cholerae co969 did not influence growth or cell morphology at low or high temperatures (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth and viability assays (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 2).

claim: BipA has been implicated in biofilm formation in some bacteria.
source: BipA has been implicated in biofilm formation in some bacteria (Grant et al., 2003; Hiramatsu et al., 2016; Neidig et al., 2013; Overhage et al., 2007), but the mechanism underlying this phenotype has remained elusive.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of VC2744 in co969 resulted in a rugose colony phenotype at 22°C.
source: Deletion of VC2744 in co969 confirmed the rugose colony phenotype from our screen at 22°C (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Figure 3C).

claim: Complementation of co969 ΔVC2744 with V. cholerae VC2744 restored the WT smooth colony morphology phenotype at 22°C.
source: Complementation of co969 ΔVC2744 with either V. cholerae VC2744 or bipA homologs from E. coli MG1655 K-12 or Pseudomonas putida KT2440 led to restoration of the WT smooth colony morphology phenotype at 22°C (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Figure 3D).

claim: Complementation of co969 ΔVC2744 with bipA homologs from E. coli MG1655 K-12 or Pseudomonas putida KT2440 restored the WT smooth colony morphology phenotype at 22°C.
source: Complementation of co969 ΔVC2744 with either V. cholerae VC2744 or bipA homologs from E. coli MG1655 K-12 or Pseudomonas putida KT2440 led to restoration of the WT smooth colony morphology phenotype at 22°C (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Figure 3D).

claim: VC2744 corresponds to the bipA ortholog in V. cholerae.
source: These results, together with the high degree of similarity between the proteins, strongly suggest that VC2744 corresponds to the bipA ortholog in V. cholerae.
evidence: Inferred from complementation experiments and sequence similarity.

claim: Deletion of bipA led to an increase in rugosity only in HapR− but not HapR+ strains.
source: Consistent with our previous data, deletion of bipA led to an increase in rugosity only in HapR− (co969 or C6706 ΔhapR) but not HapR+ strains (C6706 WT or co969:hapRc), suggesting that the effect of BipA on colony morphology is epistatic to HapR in certain V. cholerae strains (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B).

claim: The effect of BipA on colony morphology is epistatic to HapR in certain V. cholerae strains.
source: Consistent with our previous data, deletion of bipA led to an increase in rugosity only in HapR− (co969 or C6706 ΔhapR) but not HapR+ strains (C6706 WT or co969:hapRc), suggesting that the effect of BipA on colony morphology is epistatic to HapR in certain V. cholerae strains (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B).

claim: A previous V. cholerae transcriptomic survey indicated that a mutant in the biofilm regulator vqmA increased bipA levels.
source: A previous V. cholerae transcriptomic survey indicated that a mutant in the biofilm regulator vqmA increased bipA levels (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Deletion of vqmA in co969 did not phenocopy ΔbipA rugose colony morphology at low temperature.
source: However, deletion of vqmA in co969 did not phenocopy ΔbipA rugose colony morphology at low temperature, suggesting that VqmA does not affect the expression of bipA under these experimental conditions (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).

claim: VqmA does not affect the expression of bipA under the experimental conditions tested.
source: However, deletion of vqmA in co969 did not phenocopy ΔbipA rugose colony morphology at low temperature, suggesting that VqmA does not affect the expression of bipA under these experimental conditions (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).
evidence: Inferred from genetic experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).

claim: ΔvpsR and ΔvpsT mutants exhibit constitutively smooth colony morphologies.
source: To place BipA in the hierarchy of biofilm regulators in V. cholerae, we also deleted this gene in the ΔvpsR and ΔvpsT backgrounds, both of which exhibit constitutively smooth colony morphologies.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of these mutants.

claim: ΔbipA ΔvpsR and ΔbipA ΔvpsT double mutants maintained smooth colony morphology.
source: Both double mutants maintained smoothness (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C), suggesting that BipA acts upstream of VpsR and VpsT and further demonstrating rugose colony formation depends on the presence of biofilm regulatory elements.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).

claim: BipA acts upstream of VpsR and VpsT.
source: Both double mutants maintained smoothness (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C), suggesting that BipA acts upstream of VpsR and VpsT and further demonstrating rugose colony formation depends on the presence of biofilm regulatory elements.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).

claim: Rugose colony formation depends on the presence of biofilm regulatory elements.
source: Both double mutants maintained smoothness (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C), suggesting that BipA acts upstream of VpsR and VpsT and further demonstrating rugose colony formation depends on the presence of biofilm regulatory elements.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3C).

claim: bipA overexpression at 37°C led to a very subtle reduction in rugosity compared to that at 22°C.
source: A key observation was that bipA overexpression at 37°C led to a very subtle reduction in rugosity compared to that at 22°C (Figure 3D), suggesting that BipA activity is higher or more consequential at lower temperatures.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Figure 3D).

claim: BipA activity is higher or more consequential at lower temperatures.
source: A key observation was that bipA overexpression at 37°C led to a very subtle reduction in rugosity compared to that at 22°C (Figure 3D), suggesting that BipA activity is higher or more consequential at lower temperatures.
evidence: Inferred from overexpression experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: bipA transcript levels were largely unchanged between colonies grown at 37°C and 22°C.
source: Remarkably, even though bipA transcript levels were largely unchanged between colonies grown at 37°C and 22°C (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 4A), BipA protein levels were about 10 times higher at 22°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 4A).

claim: BipA protein levels were about 10 times higher at 22°C compared to 37°C.
source: Remarkably, even though bipA transcript levels were largely unchanged between colonies grown at 37°C and 22°C (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 4A), BipA protein levels were about 10 times higher at 22°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis (Figure 4B).

claim: Temperature-dependent changes in BipA levels were observed both in the presence or absence of HapR.
source: Temperature-dependent changes in BipA levels were observed both in the presence or absence of HapR (Figure 4), further suggesting that BipA regulation and its downstream effects are controlled by HapR.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis (Figure 4).

claim: Purified BipA pre-incubated at different temperatures exhibited slightly different CD curves.
source: Interestingly, purified BipA pre-incubated at different temperatures (37°C, 22°C and 15°C) exhibited slightly different CD curves (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by circular dichroism experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 4).

claim: Incubation of BipA at 37°C followed by subsequent incubation at 22°C showed the same CD pattern as for the protein incubated only at 37°C.
source: Furthermore, incubation of BipA at 37°C followed by subsequent incubation at 22°C showed the same pattern as for the protein incubated only at 37°C, suggesting that temperature-dependent protein folding changes in BipA that are likely irreversible.
evidence: Demonstrated by circular dichroism experiments.

claim: Temperature-dependent protein folding changes in BipA are likely irreversible.
source: Furthermore, incubation of BipA at 37°C followed by subsequent incubation at 22°C showed the same pattern as for the protein incubated only at 37°C, suggesting that temperature-dependent protein folding changes in BipA that are likely irreversible.
evidence: Inferred from circular dichroism experiments.

claim: Transposon mutagenesis screening for aberrantly smooth co969 colonies at 37°C identified the protease LonA as a potential repressor of BipA activity.
source: Therefore, we aimed to identify the BipA-targeting protease(s). Transposon mutagenesis screening for aberrantly smooth co969 colonies at 37°C identified the protease LonA, which has previously been reported to participate in biofilm regulation, as a potential repressor of BipA activity (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5; Supplementary file 7; Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: Identified through transposon mutagenesis screen (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5; Supplementary file 7).

claim: LonA has previously been reported to participate in biofilm regulation.
source: Therefore, we aimed to identify the BipA-targeting protease(s). Transposon mutagenesis screening for aberrantly smooth co969 colonies at 37°C identified the protease LonA, which has previously been reported to participate in biofilm regulation, as a potential repressor of BipA activity (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5; Supplementary file 7; Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Deletion of lonA in co969 led to the formation of smooth colonies at both 37°C and 22°C.
source: Deletion of VC1920 (lonA) in co969 led to the formation of smooth colonies at both 37°C and 22°C (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5B), and overexpression of lonA resulted in increased rugosity at both temperatures (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5B).

claim: Overexpression of lonA resulted in increased rugosity at both 37°C and 22°C.
source: Deletion of VC1920 (lonA) in co969 led to the formation of smooth colonies at both 37°C and 22°C (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5B), and overexpression of lonA resulted in increased rugosity at both temperatures (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology observations (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5C).

claim: BipA protein levels were unchanged in the ΔlonA background.
source: However, BipA protein levels were unchanged in the ΔlonA background (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5D), suggesting that the effect of LonA in biofilm formation does not involve BipA.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5D).

claim: The effect of LonA in biofilm formation does not involve BipA.
source: However, BipA protein levels were unchanged in the ΔlonA background (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5D), suggesting that the effect of LonA in biofilm formation does not involve BipA.
evidence: Inferred from Western blot and genetic experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 5D).

claim: LonA regulates biofilm-associated colony morphology in V. cholerae in a BipA-independent manner.
source: These data show that LonA regulates biofilm-associated colony morphology in V. cholerae, but likely in a BipA-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: In E. coli, BipA is thought to act as a ribosome assembly factor, facilitating 50S subunit biogenesis at suboptimal temperatures.
source: In E. coli, BipA is thought to act as a ribosome assembly factor, facilitating 50S subunit biogenesis at suboptimal temperatures (Choi et al., 2019; Choudhury and Flower, 2015; Gibbs et al., 2020; Krishnan and Flower, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells grown at 22°C and lacking BipA had increased proportions of subunit particles.
source: We found that cells grown at 22°C and lacking BipA had increased proportions of subunit particles (Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis (Figure 5).

claim: The 50S peak exhibited a shoulder of slower-migrating particles in ΔbipA cells at 22°C.
source: The 50S peak also exhibited a shoulder of slower-migrating particles.
evidence: Observed in sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis (Figure 5).

claim: At 37°C, no differences in ribosome profiles were observed between control and ΔbipA strains.
source: At 37°C, no differences were observed between control and mutant strain.
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis (Figure 5).

claim: The ribosome assembly data are consistent with a modest 50S assembly defect at low temperature, similar to that reported for E. coli.
source: These data are consistent with a modest 50S assembly defect at low temperature, similar to that reported for E. coli (Gibbs et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from sucrose gradient data and comparison to previous E. coli studies.

claim: Proteomic differences between co969 WT and ΔbipA were greater at 22°C than at 37°C.
source: Proteomic differences between co969 WT and ΔbipA were greater at 22°C than at 37°C, suggesting that BipA is more active or influential at lower temperatures (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative label-free proteomics (Figure 6A and B).

claim: Relative to the WT strain, 250 proteins were more abundant in ΔbipA cells at 22°C.
source: Relative to the WT strain, 250 proteins were more abundant in ΔbipA cells at 22°C, and 52 proteins were less abundant (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative label-free proteomics (Figure 6C).

claim: Relative to the WT strain, 52 proteins were less abundant in ΔbipA cells at 22°C.
source: Relative to the WT strain, 250 proteins were more abundant in ΔbipA cells at 22°C, and 52 proteins were less abundant (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative label-free proteomics (Figure 6C).

claim: The most represented differentially produced proteins in ΔbipA at 22°C were related to external cellular components and biological processes involved in localization and transport.
source: The most represented differentially produced proteins were related to external cellular components and biological processes involved in localization and transport (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative label-free proteomics (Figure 6C).

claim: A number of biofilm components were among the upregulated proteins in ΔbipA at 22°C.
source: We identified a number of biofilm components among the upregulated proteins, confirming that BipA acts to inhibit biofilm formation-associated processes at low temperatures (i.e. 22°C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative label-free proteomics.

claim: BipA acts to inhibit biofilm formation-associated processes at low temperatures.
source: We identified a number of biofilm components among the upregulated proteins, confirming that BipA acts to inhibit biofilm formation-associated processes at low temperatures (i.e. 22°C).
evidence: Inferred from proteomic data showing upregulation of biofilm proteins in ΔbipA.

claim: The co969 ΔbipA mutant exhibited 10–20% reduced motility compared to the WT strain.
source: Consistent with this finding, the co969 ΔbipA mutant exhibited 10–20% reduced motility compared to the WT strain, with motility slightly more reduced at 22°C than at 37°C (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by motility assays (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6A).

claim: Motility was slightly more reduced at 22°C than at 37°C in the co969 ΔbipA mutant.
source: Consistent with this finding, the co969 ΔbipA mutant exhibited 10–20% reduced motility compared to the WT strain, with motility slightly more reduced at 22°C than at 37°C (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by motility assays (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6A).

claim: The effect of BipA on motility is independent of the presence of HapR.
source: We observed similar phenotypes in the co969:hapRc background (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6B), indicating that the effect of BipA on motility is independent of the presence of HapR.
evidence: Demonstrated by motility assays in different genetic backgrounds (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6B).

claim: Translation of all biofilm-related proteins tested was increased in the co969 ΔbipA mutant vs. WT, especially at 22°C.
source: The results demonstrated increased translation of all biofilm-related proteins in the co969 ΔbipA mutant vs. WT, especially at 22°C (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by β-galactosidase assays with translational reporter fusions (Figure 6D).

claim: No substantial changes in translation were observed for gyrA, hfq, and mrcA in ΔbipA vs. WT.
source: Critically, no substantial changes were observed for gyrA, hfq, and mrcA, indicating that production of these proteins is largely independent of BipA.
evidence: Demonstrated by β-galactosidase assays with translational reporter fusions (Figure 6D).

claim: Production of gyrA, hfq, and mrcA is largely independent of BipA.
source: Critically, no substantial changes were observed for gyrA, hfq, and mrcA, indicating that production of these proteins is largely independent of BipA.
evidence: Inferred from β-galactosidase assays (Figure 6D).

claim: Translation of vpsR and vpsT was higher in the co969 ΔbipA background, especially at 22°C.
source: Akin to the biofilm structural genes, translation of vpsR and vpsT was higher in the co969 ΔbipA background, especially at 22°C (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by β-galactosidase assays with translational reporter fusions (Figure 6D).

claim: Transcriptional levels of vpsR and vpsT were mostly unchanged at different temperatures and between ΔbipA and WT.
source: However, compared to the biofilm structural genes, the transcriptional levels of these two major biofilm regulators were mostly unchanged at different temperatures and between ΔbipA and WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR and RNA-seq (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 3, 4 and 5).

claim: BipA influences the production of many proteins at 22°C, including key biofilm regulators.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that BipA influences the production of many proteins at 22°C, including key biofilm regulators, potentially explaining the importance of BipA in temperature-dependent formation of biofilm-associated colony morphology.
evidence: Inferred from proteomic and translational reporter data.

claim: BipA is a broadly conserved translational GTPase.
source: BipA is a broadly conserved translational GTPase whose precise cellular function has remained elusive (Gibbs and Fredrick, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A growing body of evidence indicates that BipA facilitates 50S subunit biogenesis at suboptimal temperature.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates that BipA facilitates 50S subunit biogenesis at suboptimal temperature.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in the following sentence.

claim: E. coli K12 cells lacking BipA exhibit cold sensitivity.
source: E. coli K12 cells lacking BipA exhibit cold sensitivity and accumulate immature 50S particles when grown at suboptimal temperature (Choudhury and Flower, 2015; Gibbs et al., 2020; Krishnan and Flower, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: E. coli K12 cells lacking BipA accumulate immature 50S particles when grown at suboptimal temperature.
source: E. coli K12 cells lacking BipA exhibit cold sensitivity and accumulate immature 50S particles when grown at suboptimal temperature (Choudhury and Flower, 2015; Gibbs et al., 2020; Krishnan and Flower, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mature free 30S subunits accumulate in E. coli in the absence of BipA, presumably due to a shortage of available 50S partners.
source: Recent evidence shows that mature free 30S subunits accumulate in the absence of BipA, presumably due to a shortage of available 50S partners (Gibbs et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study, with speculative language ('presumably').

claim: Compared to that of E. coli, the 50S assembly defect in V. cholerae ΔbipA is more subtle.
source: Notably, compared to that of E. coli, this 50S assembly defect in V. cholerae is more subtle, which may explain why no obvious growth defect is observed at 22°C (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of sucrose gradient data with E. coli studies.

claim: The subtle 50S assembly defect may explain why no obvious growth defect is observed in V. cholerae ΔbipA at 22°C.
source: Notably, compared to that of E. coli, this 50S assembly defect in V. cholerae is more subtle, which may explain why no obvious growth defect is observed at 22°C (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 2).
evidence: Speculative explanation based on data comparison.

claim: An increase in free mature 30S subunits and/or decrease in free mature 50S subunits would be expected to enhance translation of certain mRNAs, reduce translation of other mRNAs, and have no impact on translation of still other mRNAs.
source: An increase in free mature 30S subunits and/or decrease in free mature 50S subunits would be expected to enhance translation of certain mRNAs, reduce translation of other mRNAs, and have no impact on translation of still other mRNAs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of translation initiation mechanisms.

claim: Perturbed translation in the absence of BipA results in increased production of one or more key regulatory proteins, like VpsR and/or VpsT, leading to transcriptional activation of the entire biofilm regulon.
source: We speculate that such perturbed translation in the absence of BipA results in increased production of one or more key regulatory proteins, like VpsR and/or VpsT, leading to transcriptional activation of the entire biofilm regulon (Figure 7).
evidence: Speculative model based on experimental data.

claim: E. coli cells lacking LepA show numerous changes in protein synthesis that depend on specific mRNA features.
source: Consistent with this general model, E. coli cells lacking LepA, a related translational GTPase involved in 30S biogenesis (Gibbs et al., 2017), show numerous changes in protein synthesis that depend on specific mRNA features (Balakrishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LepA is a related translational GTPase involved in 30S biogenesis.
source: Consistent with this general model, E. coli cells lacking LepA, a related translational GTPase involved in 30S biogenesis (Gibbs et al., 2017), show numerous changes in protein synthesis that depend on specific mRNA features (Balakrishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In V. cholerae A1552, increased c-di-GMP production at low temperatures by specific diguanylate cyclases and the cold-shock gene cspV lead to higher biofilm formation.
source: In V. cholerae A1552, increased c-di-GMP production at low temperatures by specific diguanylate cyclases (DGCs) and the cold-shock gene cspV lead to higher biofilm formation (Townsley et al., 2016; Townsley and Yildiz, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The six DGCs that were induced at low temperature in V. cholerae A1552 did not appear to be differentially expressed in RNA-seq studies of co969.
source: Furthermore, the six DGCs that were induced at low temperature in V. cholerae A1552, and account for the increased biofilm production at low temperature, did not appear to be differentially expressed in our RNA-seq studies of co969.
evidence: Based on comparison of RNA-seq data with previous studies.

claim: V. cholerae El Tor and classical biotypes modulate c-di-GMP levels using different pathways.
source: Since it is known that V. cholerae El Tor and classical biotypes (HapR+ and HapR−, respectively) modulate c-di-GMP levels using different pathways (Hammer and Bassler, 2009), which in turn results in differential regulation of biofilm formation, it seems likely that the presence or absence of HapR could account for the observed differences in the temperature-dependent regulation between these V. cholerae strains.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The presence or absence of HapR could account for the observed differences in the temperature-dependent regulation between V. cholerae strains.
source: Since it is known that V. cholerae El Tor and classical biotypes (HapR+ and HapR−, respectively) modulate c-di-GMP levels using different pathways (Hammer and Bassler, 2009), which in turn results in differential regulation of biofilm formation, it seems likely that the presence or absence of HapR could account for the observed differences in the temperature-dependent regulation between these V. cholerae strains.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on previous studies and current data.

claim: HapR neither regulates BipA production nor influences the effect of ΔbipA on cell motility.
source: The data presented in this work show that HapR neither regulates BipA production (Figure 4A and B) nor influences the effect of ΔbipA on cell motility (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR, Western blot, and motility assays (Figure 4A and B; Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 6).

claim: HapR or BipA alone are sufficient to prevent rugose colony morphology.
source: Although HapR or BipA alone (HapR+ strains and high temperature or HapR− strains at low temperature, respectively) are sufficient to prevent rugose colony morphology (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B), these proteins both contribute to the repression of biofilm gene expression via transcriptional and translational control.
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic experiments (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B).

claim: HapR and BipA both contribute to the repression of biofilm gene expression via transcriptional and translational control.
source: Although HapR or BipA alone (HapR+ strains and high temperature or HapR− strains at low temperature, respectively) are sufficient to prevent rugose colony morphology (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Figure 3A and B), these proteins both contribute to the repression of biofilm gene expression via transcriptional and translational control.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and molecular data.

claim: BipA impacts many processes including virulence, competence, QS, and protein secretion.
source: Moreover, our proteomics data showed that BipA, like HapR, impacts many processes including virulence, competence, QS, and protein secretion.
evidence: Demonstrated by proteomic analysis.

claim: Biofilm formation represents one of several cellular programs whose regulation involves combined transcriptional and translational control.
source: We propose that biofilm formation represents just one of several cellular programs whose regulation involves combined transcriptional and translational control.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: BipA is highly conserved in prokaryotes.
source: Since BipA is highly conserved in prokaryotes (Gibbs and Fredrick, 2018; Leipe et al., 2002; Margus et al., 2007), it is possible that temperature-dependent control of biofilm gene expression by BipA observed in V. cholerae is conserved in other bacteria.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Temperature-dependent control of biofilm gene expression by BipA observed in V. cholerae may be conserved in other bacteria.
source: Since BipA is highly conserved in prokaryotes (Gibbs and Fredrick, 2018; Leipe et al., 2002; Margus et al., 2007), it is possible that temperature-dependent control of biofilm gene expression by BipA observed in V. cholerae is conserved in other bacteria.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation based on conservation of BipA.

claim: Deletion of bipA has been associated with increased biofilm levels in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, deletion of bipA has been associated with increased biofilm levels in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 (Neidig et al., 2013) and Bordetella holmesii (Hiramatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Deletion of bipA has been associated with increased biofilm levels in Bordetella holmesii.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, deletion of bipA has been associated with increased biofilm levels in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 (Neidig et al., 2013) and Bordetella holmesii (Hiramatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: BipA from E. coli and P. aeruginosa cross-complemented V. cholerae ΔbipA temperature-dependent phenotypes.
source: BipA from E. coli and P. aeruginosa cross-complemented V. cholerae ΔbipA temperature-dependent phenotypes (Figure 3D), further suggesting that BipA plays a similar role in protein synthesis at suboptimal temperature across various Proteobacteria.
evidence: Demonstrated by complementation experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: BipA plays a similar role in protein synthesis at suboptimal temperature across various Proteobacteria.
source: BipA from E. coli and P. aeruginosa cross-complemented V. cholerae ΔbipA temperature-dependent phenotypes (Figure 3D), further suggesting that BipA plays a similar role in protein synthesis at suboptimal temperature across various Proteobacteria.
evidence: Inferred from cross-complementation experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: In both E. coli and V. cholerae, BipA levels are regulated by temperature.
source: In both E. coli and V. cholerae, BipA levels are regulated by temperature.
evidence: Based on current data and previous studies.

claim: The basis of BipA regulation appears to be transcriptional in E. coli.
source: However, the basis of regulation appears to be transcriptional in the case of E. coli (Choi and Hwang, 2018) and post-transcriptional in the case of V. cholerae.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The basis of BipA regulation appears to be post-transcriptional in V. cholerae.
source: However, the basis of regulation appears to be transcriptional in the case of E. coli (Choi and Hwang, 2018) and post-transcriptional in the case of V. cholerae.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and Western blot data showing unchanged transcript but increased protein levels at low temperature.

claim: Steady-state levels of BipA increase substantially in V. cholerae at reduced temperature, without an increase in transcript levels.
source: Steady-state levels of BipA increase substantially in V. cholerae at reduced temperature, without an increase in transcript levels (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot and qRT-PCR (Figure 4).

claim: CD experiments suggest that BipA adopts a conformation at 37°C that makes the protein more susceptible to degradation.
source: CD experiments suggest that BipA adopts a conformation at 37°C that makes the protein more susceptible to degradation.
evidence: Inferred from circular dichroism experiments.

claim: Temperature-dependent control of BipA may be governed by the intrinsic stability of the protein in the cell.
source: These data raise the possibility that temperature-dependent control of BipA is governed by the intrinsic stability of the protein in the cell.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on CD and protein level data.

claim: BipA is crucial for resistance to the antimicrobial peptide P2 in E. coli and Salmonella spp.
source: For example, BipA is crucial for resistance to the antimicrobial peptide P2 in E. coli and Salmonella spp. (Barker et al., 2000; Sy et al., 1995), but not in V. cholerae (Mathur and Waldor, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BipA is not crucial for resistance to the antimicrobial peptide P2 in V. cholerae.
source: For example, BipA is crucial for resistance to the antimicrobial peptide P2 in E. coli and Salmonella spp. (Barker et al., 2000; Sy et al., 1995), but not in V. cholerae (Mathur and Waldor, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Recent findings suggest a role of BipA in promoting biofilm dispersion in V. cholerae.
source: Our study supports and provides an explanation for recent findings suggesting a role of BipA in promoting biofilm dispersion in V. cholerae (Bridges et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.
